title: The disordered logistic map
abstract: The logistic map is a quintessential model in the study of low-dimensional chaos. High-dimensional chaos, on the other hand, presents itself in disordered systems with many interacting and heterogeneously coupled components. Here, we formulate a system of many logistic maps, interacting through disordered couplings. Using a combination of dynamic mean-field theory, random matrix theory and numerical simulations, we show that even the smallest amount of disorder can remove the period-doubling cascade in the conventional logistic map. Instead we find a transition to high-dimensional chaos, marked by an oscillatory instability not previously reported for disordered systems. We also show that with sufficiently strong homogeneous coupling between the maps one recovers elements of the conventional period-doubling cascade. Our findings indicate that well-known phenomena in dynamical systems can be fragile in the face of disorder. At the same time, new phenomena emerge that are neither found in simple low-dimensional dynamics nor in high-dimensional disordered systems.
summary: This work analyzes the chaotic dynamics of the disordered logistic map, showing that disorder fundamentally alters the transition to chaos by suppressing the classic period-doubling cascade. Using mean-field theory and RMT, the authors identify new instability regimes, such as oscillatory chaos, that characterize the system's behavior in the presence of quenched disorder.
main_problem: The paper investigates how introducing disorder affects the transition to chaos in low-dimensional dynamical systems, specifically by coupling multiple logistic maps.
main_result: Small amounts of disorder can eliminate the conventional period-doubling cascade, leading instead to a direct transition to a new high-dimensional chaotic state. New phenomena emerge that are not present in simple low-dimensional or standard high-dimensional disordered systems.
method: The analysis employs dynamic mean-field theory, random matrix theory (RMT), and stability analysis based on the eigenvalues of the reduced Jacobian matrix.
model_or_system: The primary model is the disordered logistic map, defined by coupled discrete-time maps with quenched random interaction coefficients. The analysis is extended to the disordered Hénon map.
key_observables: Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE), eigenvalue spectrum (checking for crossings at $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=-1$), and the Kaplan-Yorke dimension ($D_{KY}$).
important_parameters: The control parameters include the map parameter $r$, the disorder strength $\sigma$, and the homogeneous coupling strength $\mu$.
main_assumptions: Assumptions include the absence of correlations among disorder coefficients and using approximations for the eigenvalue spectrum edge derived from RMT.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate stability diagrams showing regions for different instabilities (May-Wigner, OC), and eigenvalue spectra demonstrating the bulk continuum of the reduced Jacobian matrix.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the stability boundaries by examining the eigenvalue spectrum of the coupled system. It contrasts the expected period-doubling route to chaos with transitions governed by bulk eigenvalue crossings (OC instability) or linear instability (May-Wigner instability).
why_interesting: The study of how disorder fundamentally alters universal transitions (like period-doubling) is highly relevant to understanding critical phenomena and phase transitions in complex, disordered quantum or classical many-body systems.

The dashed line is the onset of the May–Wigner instability, where the eigenvalue spectrum of the reduced Ja- cobian spreads beyond λ = 1. We continue this line as a series of dots away from the fixed-point phase, where it is no longer strictly valid, but is used to distinguish regions of the diagram with different behaviours. The solid line indicates the onset of the oscillatory chaotic (OC) instability (left-most bulk eigenvalue crossing −1). FIG. 2. Eigenvalue spectrum of the reduced Jacobian ma- trix in the fixed-point regime. Blue crosses are the result of a single numerical experiment (N = 4000), the solid red line is from Eq. (3). In the stable phase the spectrum of the re- duced Jacobian comes arbitrarily close to the point +1 in the complex plane (right-hand side tip of the spectrum). The fixed-point solution becomes unstable when eigenvalues stray outside the unit circle (dashed black line). System parame- ters: r = 1.6, σ = 0.8.

FIG. 3. Stability diagram for the model with additional ho- mogeneous coupling [Eq. (4)], at fixed σ = 0.2. The dashed line is the May–Wigner instability as before, and the solid line is the OC instability (bulk eigenvalue leaving the unit disk at λ = −1). The dot-dashed line indicates where in parameter space the outlier eigenvalue exits the unit disk (at λ = −1). The LLE Λ1 is shown in relief (blue Λ1 < 0, red Λ1 > 0). We find no chaos as a result of the outlier eigenvalue leaving the unit disk (Λ1 is found to be negative in the region between the dot-dashed and solid lines).
